title: Capacity for Grade 2: Litres, the Measuring Jug and Estimate-Then-Check + Free Quiz
meta_title: Capacity Grade 2 Litres: Jug & Half-Litre Guide
meta_desc: Teach capacity to Grade 2 in litres: read a measuring jug, compare holds-more, estimate then check, plus a free 8-question quiz and printable worksheet.
excerpt: A one-litre water bottle, a half-litre milk packet and a kitchen jug are all your Grade 2 child needs to understand capacity. Here is how I teach litres and half-litres, holds-more versus holds-less, and the estimate-then-check habit — with a quick quiz at the end.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Stand a Grade 2 child in front of two containers — a tall thin glass and a short wide bowl — and ask which one holds more. Most will point at the tall glass, every time, because it looks bigger. That single wrong guess is the whole reason capacity is worth teaching carefully. Learning about capacity for Grade 2 in litres is really about one honest lesson: your eyes lie, so you pour and you check. In this guide I will show you how I teach the litre and the half-litre, how to read a measuring jug, and the estimate-then-check habit that makes it all stick.

You do not need lab equipment. A clear plastic measuring jug from any kitchen shop for about ₹120, a one-litre water bottle, an empty half-litre milk packet, a bucket and a mug will carry you through the entire topic.

What capacity actually means at Grade 2

Capacity is how much a container can hold when it is full. That is it. At this age we are not weighing anything and we are not measuring length — we are talking only about the amount of liquid that fits inside. Keep the language clean: a container holds more or holds less, and when it is full to the top it is holding its full capacity.

The word children already half-know is litre, because they have seen it on bottles. Lean on that. A standard water bottle is one litre. A milk packet is often half a litre. Point at the printed ‘1 L’ or ‘500 ml’ on real packaging — it makes the unit feel real rather than like a school word.

The litre and the half-litre

Two units are plenty for Grade 2: the litre (written l or L) and the half-litre. A half-litre is exactly half of a litre — pour a full one-litre bottle into two identical glasses so each gets the same, and each glass holds half a litre. Doing that pour once, with the child’s own hands, teaches more than ten pictures in a book.

Reading a measuring jug

A measuring jug is the single best tool for this topic. It has lines up the side — the markings — and each line tells you how much liquid is inside. Teach your child to read the jug at the line where the water sits, with the jug on a flat table and their eyes level with the liquid, not looking down from above.

Start simple. Fill to the half-litre mark and ask, ‘how much is in the jug now?’ Then top it up to the one-litre line. Then pour some out and read the new level. The skill is reading the number next to the water line — nothing more complicated than that at Grade 2.

  • Put the jug on a flat surface, never held in the air.
  • Bend down so your eyes are level with the water.
  • Read the marking closest to the top of the liquid.
  • Say it out loud: ‘half a litre’, ‘one litre’.

Holds more, holds less

Once the jug makes sense, comparing containers becomes a game. Take that tall glass and short bowl from the start, fill each to the brim, then pour each in turn into the measuring jug and read the marks. The bowl usually wins, and the surprise on a child’s face is the lesson landing. Order three or four containers from holds-least to holds-most and you have covered comparison completely.

ContainerRough capacityHolds more or less than 1 litre?
Tea cupAbout a quarter litreLess
Milk packetHalf a litreLess
Water bottleOne litreSame
Small bucketAbout five litresMore

Estimate, then check

Here is the habit I care about most, and the one worksheets often skip. Before pouring anything, the child guesses: ‘I think the mug holds less than half a litre.’ Then they pour into the jug and check. Guess first, measure second. A wrong guess is not a failure — it is the moment they learn something, because the gap between what they expected and what the jug shows is exactly where understanding grows.

One honest caveat from teaching this to seven-year-olds: do not correct the estimate before they measure. Let them commit to a guess out loud, even a silly one, then let the jug settle the argument. If you tell them the answer first, the estimate becomes pointless and the whole exercise turns into copying.

Everyday practice that costs nothing

  • At breakfast, ask whether their glass holds more or less than the milk packet.
  • Filling a bucket for mopping? Ask how many one-litre bottles it will take, then count as you pour.
  • In the kitchen, let them read the jug when a recipe needs half a litre of water.

A simple week of capacity

Ten minutes a day beats a long Sunday session. Two days on reading the jug, two days on holds-more versus holds-less with real containers, one day on estimate-then-check, and the weekend for written practice on paper so they have to picture the jug without one in front of them. That last step, imagining the markings, is where you see whether the idea has truly stuck.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a short, free quiz covering exactly what we did here — litres and half-litres, reading a jug, holds-more, and estimate-then-check. Let your child try it and read the explanations together for anything they miss. quiz.title: Grade 2 Capacity Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on litres, half-litres, reading a measuring jug and comparing capacity. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: Which of these is a unit for measuring capacity?
questions.explanation: Capacity is how much liquid a container holds, and it is measured in litres. Centimetres measure length and kilograms measure weight.

questions.q: How many half-litres make one litre?
questions.explanation: A half-litre is half of a litre, so two half-litres together make one full litre.

questions.q: A measuring jug shows water up to the half-litre line. How much water is in it?
questions.explanation: You read the jug at the line where the water sits. The water is at the half-litre mark, so it holds half a litre.

questions.q: Which container most likely holds MORE than one litre?
questions.explanation: A bucket holds several litres, far more than a cup, a milk packet or a spoon.

questions.q: A water bottle holds one litre. About how much does a small milk packet usually hold?
questions.explanation: A common small milk packet holds about half a litre, which is less than the one-litre bottle.

questions.q: The best way to read a measuring jug is to:
options: Hold it up high and look down
Put it on a table and look at eye level
questions.explanation: Stand the jug on a flat table and bring your eyes level with the water, then read the nearest marking.

questions.q: Before you pour water into a jug to measure it, what should you do first?
options: Empty the jug into the sink
questions.explanation: Estimate first, then check by pouring and reading the jug. Guessing first is what makes the measuring worthwhile.

questions.q: Two glasses each hold half a litre. How much do they hold together?
questions.explanation: Half a litre plus half a litre makes one whole litre.

faq.q: What is the difference between capacity and weight for a Grade 2 child?
faq.a: Capacity is how much liquid a container can hold, measured in litres. Weight is how heavy something is, measured in kilograms. At Grade 2 keep them separate — capacity is only about pouring and filling, not about how heavy the water feels.

faq.q: Do I need special equipment to teach capacity at home?
faq.a: No. A clear plastic measuring jug, a one-litre water bottle, an empty half-litre milk packet, a mug and a bucket cover the whole topic. Real kitchen containers work better than pictures because the child pours the water themselves.

faq.q: Why does my child think a tall thin glass holds more than a wide bowl?
faq.a: Because taller looks bigger to young eyes. This is exactly why we pour into a measuring jug and read the marks — measuring settles the argument that guessing cannot, and the surprise helps the idea stick.

faq.q: What does estimate-then-check mean and why does it matter?
faq.a: The child guesses how much a container holds before measuring, then pours into the jug to see if the guess was right. The gap between the guess and the real answer is where the learning happens, so let them commit to a guess before you correct anything.
